This guideline is for adults and children in non-traumatic cardiac arrest. See the ‘cardiac arrest secondary to
trauma’ guideline if the cardiac arrest is secondary to trauma.
Initial actions (the first 1-4 minutes)
Perform continuous chest compressions while the defibrillator is being attached and charged.
Defibrillate immediately if the cardiac rhythm is VF or VT using a single shock and immediately
recommence chest compressions:
Maximum joule setting for an adult.
See the paediatric drug dose tables for joule settings for a child.
Place an SGA and commence ventilation, preferably using a timing indicator.
Subsequent actions
Perform two-minute cycles of high performance CPR between rhythm checks.
Administer adrenaline IV every four minutes:
1 mg IV for an adult.
See the paediatric drug dose tables for a child.
Consider placing an ETT.
Establish a team leader and utilise the cardiac arrest checklist.
If the rhythm is VF or VT
Defibrillate using single shocks every two minutes.
Immediately recommence chest compressions after each shock.
If in VF or VT after three shocks, including shocks delivered prior to ambulance arrival:
Administer amiodarone:
300 mg IV for an adult.
See the paediatric drug dose tables for a child.
Consider changing to anterior/posterior pad placement or performing double sequential
defibrillation.
If in VF or VT after six shocks, including shocks delivered prior to ambulance arrival, administer a second
dose of amiodarone:
150 mg IV for an adult.
See the paediatric drug dose tables for a child.

Seek clinical advice if VF or VT persists.
If torsades de pointes is present or has occurred
Withhold amiodarone.
Administer magnesium IV:
10 mmol (2.5 g) over 1-2 minutes for an adult.
See the paediatric drug dose tables for a child.
Repeat once if torsades de pointes recurs or persists.
If the patient is in PEA
Correct immediately reversible causes.
Administer 0.9% sodium chloride IV:
1-2 litres IV for an adult.
20-40 ml/kg IV for a child.
If patient movement is interfering with resuscitation
Administer 1 mg/kg of ketamine IV, up to a maximum of 150 mg.
This may be repeated once if required.
If significant movement continues, consider administering 2 mg/kg of rocuronium IV up to a maximum of
200 mg, provided an ETT has been placed, and the position confirmed using ETCO2.
Backup
Backup from an ICP/CCP should be requested.
Cardiac arrest checklist
Team leader identified.
Roles allocated and confirmed.
CPR feedback device and metronome on if available.
Defibrillator screen visible to the team leader.
Airway adjunct or ETT in place and ventilation adequate.

Additional information
Deciding to start resuscitation
Resuscitation should start unless there is a clear reason not to. Clear reasons for not starting resuscitation
include:
Signs of rigor mortis or post-mortem lividity.
A clear advance directive not to receive resuscitation for cardiac arrest.
Scenarios where resuscitation is futile or clearly not in the best interest of the patient. Examples
include unwitnessed cardiac arrest with asystole as the initial rhythm, patients who are dying from
cancer and patients with severe life-limiting disease.
Ambulance personnel must consider all available information, including the patient’s known wishes (for
example, their advance directive) and act in what they believe is the best interest of the patient.
If there is doubt regarding the appropriateness of a resuscitation attempt, resuscitation should begin
while further information is gained.
Nobody has the right to demand resuscitation on behalf of a patient, including those with an Enduring
Power of Attorney and family/whānau, but the known wishes of the patient must be considered.
Family/whānau do not have the right to decline resuscitation on behalf of a patient unless they have an
Enduring Power of Attorney. See the ‘treatment and/or transport without informed consent’ guideline
for more information.
There must be clear documentation regarding decisions made.

Deciding to stop resuscitation
There is no absolute time at which it is possible to say that further resuscitation is futile. Stopping
resuscitation requires clinical judgement on the likelihood of survival, considering the following:
The cause of the cardiac arrest.
Whether or not the cardiac arrest was witnessed.
Whether or not there was bystander CPR.
The response time.
The initial rhythm.
The total estimated time in cardiac arrest.
The end tidal CO2.
Whether ROSC has occurred at any time.
The patient’s comorbidities.
Deciding to stop resuscitation: EMTs
Resuscitation must continue until a Paramedic, ICP or CCP arrives and makes a decision to stop, or advice
is received via the Clinical Desk that it is appropriate to stop. If backup is not available, and the Clinical
Desk cannot be contacted:
If the arrest was unwitnessed and no shock is advised, the prognosis is very poor and it is appropriate
to stop resuscitation if there are no signs of ROSC 20 minutes after the onset of resuscitation by
ambulance personnel.
For other circumstances it is appropriate to stop resuscitation if there are no signs of ROSC 40
minutes after the onset of resuscitation by ambulance personnel.
Deciding to stop resuscitation: Paramedics, ICPs and CCPs
It is usually appropriate to stop resuscitation:
20 minutes after the onset of resuscitation by ambulance personnel in poor prognosis scenarios.
40 minutes after the onset of resuscitation by ambulance personnel in good prognosis scenarios.
Earlier than described above, if it becomes clear that it was inappropriate to have commenced
resuscitation, or the rhythm has deteriorated into asystole for more than a few minutes despite
resuscitation.

Movement during cardiac arrest
The patient may move during cardiac arrest if cerebral blood flow is being maintained by very good CPR.
This can cause personnel to believe that the patient is not in cardiac arrest and may lead to delayed
defibrillation and/or inappropriate pauses in CPR.
It is appropriate to briefly pause CPR to confirm the patient is in cardiac arrest.
If rocuronium is administered, neuromuscular blockade will continue if sustained ROSC is achieved and
the patient will then require an adequate level of sedation.
The prognosis of cardiac arrest
There is no one factor that can be used to determine the prognosis of an individual patient in cardiac arrest.
Multiple factors must be considered, noting that in most patients there will be a mixture of prognostic factors.

Poor prognostic factors
Secondary cardiac arrest
Unwitnessed
No bystander CPR
Response time > 8 minutes
Initial rhythm asystole or PEA
Time in cardiac arrest > 30 minutes
Severe comorbidities
Living in aged residential care
Age > 80 years
ETCO2 < 15 mmHg or falling despite CPR
Good prognostic factors
Primary cardiac arrest
Witnessed
Bystander CPR
Response time < 8 minutes
Initial rhythm VT or VF
Time in cardiac arrest < 30 minutes
No severe comorbidities
Living independently
Age ≤ 80 years
ETCO2 > 25 mmHg with CPR
Severe comorbidities are chronic diseases that significantly limit a patient’s life expectancy. Examples
include dementia, severe COPD, severe heart failure, a requirement for aged residential care and
metastatic cancer with weight loss.
The reactivity of the patient’s pupils during and immediately following cardiac arrest is not prognostic and
there is no role for including pupil reactivity in decision making.
High performance CPR
High performance CPR encompasses the concepts of:
Optimising chest compression depth, rate, and recoil.

Minimising interruptions to chest compressions.
Avoiding over-ventilation.
Perform chest compressions at a rate of 100-120/minute, ensuring adequate depth and complete recoil.
CPR should be performed for two minute cycles between rhythm checks. The person performing chest
compressions should ideally change every two minutes, or earlier if tired.
A CPR feedback device and/or metronome must be used if available.
Pauses in CPR for rhythm checks, defibrillation or ventilation should be minimised, and usually last no
longer than three seconds. A pause of up to 10 seconds is permitted for a pulse check in PEA.
The person performing chest compressions should hover approximately 5 cm above the patient’s chest
during the pause.

Ventilation in high performance CPR
Ventilation has a low priority during the first few minutes of resuscitation if the patient has had a primary
cardiac arrest.

Once ventilation has commenced, the ventilation rate should be no more than 10/minute, as rates higher
than this increase intrathoracic pressure and therefore reduce venous return during CPR.
When ventilation is provided via a bag and mask:
For an adult the CPR compression to ventilation ratio is 30:2. This ratio prioritises chest compressions
on the basis that an adult is most likely to have had a primary cardiac arrest. If an adult has had a
cardiac arrest secondary to asphyxiation or respiratory failure, alter the ratio to 15:2.
For a child the CPR compression to ventilation ratio is 15:2 (exception – the ratio is 3:1 for newborns).
The 15:2 ratio reduces the priority of chest compressions on the basis that a child is most likely to
have had a cardiac arrest secondary to respiratory failure. If a child has had a primary cardiac arrest,
alter the ratio to 30:2.
When ventilation is being provided via an SGA or ETT:
Perform continuous chest compressions and ventilate adults and children at a rate of 10/minute,
preferably using a ventilation timing light.
If continuous chest compressions clearly impair ventilation via an SGA, interrupt the chest
compressions to provide ventilations using the ratios described above.
Intubation is not a high priority during the initial management of cardiac arrest. If ROSC has not been
achieved within 10 minutes, intubation with an ETT may occur provided this does not interrupt chest
compressions.
IV access and medicines
Gaining IV access and administering medicines has a lower priority than providing high performance CPR.
IV access is preferred over IO access. Clinical judgement should be used and IO access should usually be
obtained if IV access cannot be gained, and resuscitation is ongoing.
All doses should be flushed with a running line of 0.9% sodium chloride or a minimum of 20 ml 0.9%
sodium chloride.
End tidal CO2
End tidal CO2 (ETCO2) is a marker of the blood flow being achieved during CPR. With good CPR an
ETCO2 of greater than 20 mmHg should usually be achieved, unless there is an obstruction to blood flow,
for example from a pulmonary embolus or tension pneumothorax.
ETCO2 must be used to confirm ETT placement and must be continuously measured if the patient has
been intubated with an ETT.

ETCO2 should be continuously measured if the patient is being ventilated via an SGA, noting that the
ETCO2 will be reduced if there is significant leak around the cuff. In this setting the trend of the ETCO2 is
more important than individual recordings.
ETCO2 may be measured if the patient is being ventilated via a face mask, noting that the ETCO2 will be
reduced if there is significant leak around the mask. In this setting the trend of the ETCO2 is more
important than individual recordings.
A sudden increase in ETCO2 is usually an indicator that ROSC has occurred.
A falling ETCO2 despite CPR is a poor prognostic factor and must prompt a focus on ensuring high
performance CPR is being provided and the ventilation rate is at or below 10/minute.
An ETCO2 of less than 15 mmHg despite CPR is a very poor prognostic factor.
Defibrillation
Pad placement and adherence is important. It is worth taking the extra time to ensure the pads are
placed in the ideal location and are well adhered.
Routinely place pads in the anterior/posterior position for small children and morbidly obese patients.
If VF or VT persists or recurs after three shocks, consider whether it is recurrent, or refractory. Because
CPR is initiated immediately after each shock, it is not always possible to differentiate:
VF or VT that is successfully reverted with each shock and then recurs, and thus is recurrent, versus
VF or VT that is not successfully reverted with each shock, and thus is refractory.
If VF or VT is clearly recurrent, changing the defibrillation strategy is not required.
If VF or VT is clearly or possibly refractory, the defibrillation strategy should be changed.
The two options when changing the defibrillation strategy are:
Anterior/posterior pad placement, or
Double sequential defibrillation (DSD).
Anterior/posterior pad placement is the preferred approach when one manual defibrillator is present, or if
the team are not fully trained in DSD.
DSD is the preferred approach when two manual defibrillators are present, and the team is fully trained in
DSD.

Double sequential defibrillation
Double sequential defibrillation (DSD) is the provision of two sequential (approximately one second apart)
shocks, using two manual defibrillators, with the pads attached in two different vectors, one in the anterolateral vector and the other in the antero-posterior vector.
When providing DSD:
Only those personnel specifically trained in the technique may provide DSD.
Use only manual defibrillators.
Ensure none of the pads are touching.
One person must discharge both defibrillators sequentially, to avoid simultaneous defibrillation.

Pulseless electrical activity (PEA)
PEA is present when a patient in cardiac arrest has a rhythm that should be associated with cardiac output
but is not. PEA is a clinical condition and not an abnormal rhythm.
PEA is often secondary to a non-cardiac problem. The history immediately prior to cardiac arrest is very
important in helping to determine what the cause may be.
Potentially reversible causes of PEA include:
Hypoxia.
Hypothermia.
Hypovolaemia (including anaphylaxis).
Hyper/hypokalaemia (and other metabolic abnormalities).
Tension pneumothorax.
Tamponade (cardiac).
Toxins (poisoning).
Thrombosis (pulmonary and coronary).

Some references include hydrogen ions (acidosis) and hypoglycaemia in the list of causes of PEA.
However, neither of these cause cardiac arrest in the absence of another clinical problem, even when
severe. Hypoglycaemia should be ruled out following ROSC.
Consideration should be given to transporting the patient to hospital with CPR en route if a potentially
reversible cause is identified that cannot be treated at the scene. To be successful, such a decision must
be made very early in the resuscitation attempt.
It is common for PEA to degenerate into asystole with time. During this process slow (less than
30/minute) broad complexes may be present. This is treated as asystole and not PEA.
Survival is rare if the rhythm deteriorates from PEA into asystole despite resuscitation and prolonged
resuscitation attempts in this setting are usually inappropriate.
In general, patients that survive cardiac arrest with an initial rhythm of PEA do so because the underlying
problem is immediately identified and corrected.
If the patient remains in PEA despite resuscitation attempts, consider the possibility that there is cardiac
output that cannot be detected clinically. In this setting stop chest compressions and observe the ETCO2
for one minute while ventilating at a rate of 10/minute:
If the ETCO2 rapidly falls to below 10 mmHg the patient is in cardiac arrest.
If the ETCO2 is maintained at or above 10 mmHg, the patient has low cardiac output and should be
treated accordingly.
If available, ultrasound can be useful to assess for cardiac activity and reversible causes of PEA arrest.
Asystole
Confirm the rhythm is asystole by checking:
The cables.
The leads.
Which lead is selected on the screen.
The amplitude.
Exclude bradycardia which can look like asystole at a glance, particularly in children.
Survival from cardiac arrest with an initial rhythm of asystole is rare and prolonged resuscitation attempts
in this setting are usually inappropriate, particularly if the cardiac arrest was unwitnessed.

Attach and use a defibrillator immediately. It is acceptable to use the defibrillator in automatic mode until
additional personnel arrive.
Perform CPR with a focus on chest compressions, utilising bystanders to help.
Interventions such as IV access or intubation are not a priority and should only occur after additional
trained personnel arrive.
Transport to hospital with CPR en route
Transport to hospital with CPR en route should be rare because:
There is no convincing evidence it improves patient outcomes.
The quality of the resuscitation attempt (particularly the quality of CPR) is usually compromised,
unless mechanical CPR is available.
Unrestrained personnel are at risk in the back of a moving ambulance.
However, a small number of patients may benefit from transport to hospital with CPR en route,
particularly if there is a potentially reversible cause that ambulance personnel are unable to treat (for
example, hypothermia and poisoning). To be successful, such a decision must be made very early in the
resuscitation attempt.
Provide as much pre-hospital warning as possible.
Response and/or transport by helicopter
It is uncommon for a helicopter to locate a patient within a timeframe that provides meaningful clinical
benefit.
Response by helicopter may be indicated if the patient is suspected to be in cardiac arrest and the
helicopter will arrive on scene:
Prior to a road ambulance resource and a resuscitation attempt is expected, or
To deliver a CCP skill that will likely improve the patient’s outcome (for example, cardiac arrest
secondary to drowning).
Mechanical CPR
Mechanical CPR does not usually have a role early in cardiac arrest but should be considered when:
It is not safe to perform manual chest compressions, for example in a moving ambulance.
There is insufficient room or personnel to perform chest compressions.
A prolonged resuscitation attempt is anticipated.

Defibrillator failure action list
Use this action list if a defibrillator fails and there is not another defibrillator (including an AED)
immediately available. At each defibrillator intervention, pause briefly to determine if the problem has
been fixed.
Task specific personnel to focus on resuscitating the patient.
Task specific personnel to focus on troubleshooting the defibrillator.
Ensure the pads are attached and connected.
Ensure all components of the defibrillator are physically connected.
Ensure the ECG leads are attached.
Change the lead shown on the screen so that the rhythm is visible.
Attach and connect a new set of pads.
Switch to automatic mode if in manual mode.
Turn the defibrillator off for 30 seconds and turn it back on again.
Seek urgent clinical advice if the situation is not resolved.
Cardiac arrest in special situations
Cardiac arrest secondary to drowning
Prioritise the ventilation aspect of CPR and use a CPR ratio of 15:2 unless an ETT is in place.
Place an ETT if ROSC is not achieved in the first few minutes.
IV medicines have a very low priority.
See the ‘drowning’ guideline for additional information.
Cardiac arrest secondary to hanging
Prioritise the ventilation aspect of CPR and use a CPR ratio of 15:2 unless an ETT is in place.
Cervical spine immobilisation is not routinely required. This is because clinically significant cervical spine
injury following hanging is extremely rare unless the patient has fallen the height of their body.
The survival rate is low, but survivors usually come from the group that are in PEA and get ROSC within 510 minutes with good CPR alone.

Prolonged resuscitation in the presence of asystole is inappropriate.
IV medicines have a very low priority.
Cardiac arrest secondary to asthma
Focus on using a ventilation rate of only 6/minute to avoid dynamic hyperinflation (gas trapping).
IV adrenaline has a high priority.
Exclude tension pneumothorax, noting this is rare. Needle chest decompression carries a significant risk
of causing pneumothorax and finger thoracostomy is the preferred technique if chest decompression is
required.
Cardiac arrest secondary to anaphylaxis
IV adrenaline has a high priority.
If the patient is in PEA and not immediately responding to resuscitation, escalate the adrenaline doses:
For an adult escalate the second dose to 3 mg, the third dose to 5 mg and then revert to standard 1
mg dosing.
For a child escalate the doses following the same principle.
0.9% sodium chloride IV has a high priority:
For an adult administer 2-3 litres of 0.9% sodium chloride IV.
For a child administer 40-60 ml/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride IV.
Cardiac arrest secondary to cyclic antidepressant poisoning
The cardiac toxicity of cyclic antidepressants is partly caused by blockade of sodium channels within the
heart and may be reduced by a large bolus of sodium ions.
Administer 8.4% sodium bicarbonate IV:
100 ml for an adult.
2 ml/kg for a child.
Administer 0.9% sodium chloride IV:
1-2 litres for an adult.
20-40 ml/kg for a child.

Do not administer amiodarone because it can be associated with severe worsening of shock without
resolution of the rhythm.
Cardiac arrest during pregnancy greater than 20 weeks
In pregnancy where gestation is greater than 20 weeks, the uterus may impede venous return through the
inferior vena cava in the supine position. Manually displace the uterus to the left to alleviate this.
Consider transporting the patient with CPR en route (focusing on good chest compressions) if ROSC is
not immediately achieved and time to a hospital is less than 10 minutes. Provide as much pre-hospital
warning as possible. In this setting the primary reason for emergency caesarean section is to improve the
chance of survival for the mother.
Cardiac arrest secondary to hypothermia
See the ‘hypothermia’ guideline.
Cardiac arrest secondary to hyperkalaemia
See the ‘hyperkalaemia’ guideline.
Cardiac arrest secondary to opiate poisoning
The best treatment is CPR that includes a focus on ventilation.
There is no role for naloxone because cardiac arrest is secondary to respiratory arrest and once cardiac
arrest has occurred naloxone has no useful effect. If ROSC occurs, naloxone should still not be
administered because it may be associated with seizures, hypertension, pulmonary oedema or severe
agitation.
Cardiac arrest and implanted defibrillators/pacemakers
Implanted defibrillators and pacemakers are usually situated in the soft tissue under the left clavicle.
Place defibrillation pads at least 8 cm from the implanted device if possible and consider utilising the
anterior/posterior position.

Cardiac arrest occurring in infants during sleep
Prioritise the ventilation aspect of CPR using a CPR ratio of 15:2.
Beware of misdiagnosing severe bradycardia as asystole.
Survival is very low, but survivors tend to come from the group of patients that get ROSC within 5-10

Prolonged resuscitation in the presence of asystole is inappropriate.
IV medicines have a very low priority.
Transport to hospital with CPR en route is inappropriate.

Mechanism of action
Adrenaline stimulates alpha and beta receptors, with the predominant effects occurring at alpha 1, beta 1
and beta 2 receptors.
Alpha 1 stimulation causes smooth muscle contraction, vasoconstriction of blood vessels and stimulation
of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Beta 1 stimulation causes an increase in inotropy (cardiac contractility), an increase in chronotropy (heart
rate) and an increase in dromotropy (speed of electrical conduction within the heart).
Beta 2 stimulation causes smooth muscle relaxation, skeletal muscle vasodilation, bronchodilation, and
stabilisation of mast cell membranes, reducing histamine release.
Authorised practice levels
EMTs: nebulised, IM, IN and topical adrenaline.
Paramedics: all of the above and adrenaline IV for cardiac arrest.
ICPs and CCPs: all indications and all routes.
Indications
Cardiac arrest.
Anaphylaxis.
Severe asthma.
Imminent respiratory arrest from COPD.
Bradycardia with moderate or severe cardiovascular compromise.
Blood pressure support if unresponsive to metaraminol.
Septic shock, cardiogenic shock, and neurogenic shock, unresponsive to 0.9% sodium chloride IV and
metaraminol IV.
Stridor causing moderate or severe respiratory distress.
IN for clinically significant epistaxis.
Topical for clinically significant bleeding from a wound.

Contraindications
None.
Cautions
Myocardial ischaemia. Adrenaline will increase myocardial oxygen consumption.
Tachydysrhythmias. Adrenaline will usually make tachydysrhythmias worse.
Use in pregnancy or when breastfeeding
Safe and should be administered when indicated.
Dosage
The dose of adrenaline is dependent on the indication and the route. See the individual guideline.
Administration
Topical: dilute each mg of adrenaline to a total of 10 ml using 0.9% sodium chloride. This solution is
1:10,000 and contains 0.1 mg/ml. Apply topically in addition to direct pressure.
IN: dilute each mg of adrenaline to a total of 10 ml using 0.9% sodium chloride. This solution is 1:10,000
and contains 0.1 mg/ml. Administer the appropriate dose into each bleeding nostril using a mucosal
atomising device, in addition to direct pressure.
Nebulised: administer undiluted.
IM: administer undiluted. The preferred IM site is the lateral thigh. If this site is not suitable use the lateral
upper arm.
Cardiac arrest:
Adults and children whose weight has been rounded to 50 kg or more: administer undiluted as an IV
bolus.
Children whose weight has been rounded to 40 kg or less: dilute 1 mg of adrenaline to a total of 10
ml using 0.9% sodium chloride. This solution is 1:10,000 and contains 0.1 mg/ml. Draw up the dose
from this solution and administer as an IV bolus.

Mechanism of action
Amiodarone is an antidysrhythmic with a broad spectrum of activity.
Amiodarone has predominantly class III activity. It prolongs the action potential duration, reduces
automaticity and prolongs the refractory period of atrial, nodal and ventricular tissues.
The electrophysiological effects result in a reduction in abnormal electrical activity (for example ectopy), a
reduction in electrical conduction, a reduction in heart rate and a stabilisation of the SA and AV nodes.
Amiodarone also causes a small increase in coronary blood flow (although this is not usually clinically
significant) and a reduction in myocardial oxygen consumption by reducing inotropy (the force of cardiac
contraction).
Authorised practice levels
Paramedics: cardiac arrest.
ICPs and CCPs: all indications.
Indications
Cardiac arrest with VF or VT after three shocks.
Adults with sustained VT in the absence of cardiac arrest.
Adults with moderate cardiovascular compromise as a result of atrial fibrillation, where the ventricular rate
is predominantly greater than 130/minute and metoprolol PO is contraindicated.
Adults with moderate cardiovascular compromise as a result of atrial flutter, where the ventricular rate is
predominantly greater than 130/minute.
Contraindications
Known severe allergy.
Known severe allergy to iodine.
VT secondary to cyclic antidepressant poisoning. In this setting amiodarone administration can be
associated with severe worsening of shock, without resolution of the rhythm.
If torsades de pointes is present or has occurred.

Administration
Cardiac arrest: administer IV undiluted as a bolus.
Tachydysrhythmia:
Place 300 mg of amiodarone in 100 ml of 5% glucose and label. 1 drop/second via a standard IV

amiodarone has been administered.
An IV infusion over 30 minutes is the preferred method of administration. However, it is acceptable to
dilute 300 mg of amiodarone to a total volume of 20-30 ml using 5% glucose or 0.9% sodium
chloride. Administer this IV over 30 minutes and slow the rate of infusion if hypotension occurs.

Hypotension.

Bradydysrhythmia.

5-10 minutes.

1-4 hours after a single dose.

particularly when more than one dose has been administered. This is why many references quote a halflife of 10-60 days, but the clinical duration of effect is much shorter than this.

Pharmacokinetics
Amiodarone is metabolised in the liver.

Common interactions
May potentiate the action of cyclic antidepressants in cyclic poisoning.
May cause bradycardia following reversion of dysrhythmia if the patient is taking a beta-blocker and/or a
centrally acting calcium channel blocker (for example diltiazem).
Additional information
If the indication is atrial fibrillation causing moderate cardiovascular compromise, the goal of treatment is
to control the ventricular rate and not to revert the rhythm to sinus rhythm, although treatment with
amiodarone may result in reversion of the rhythm to sinus rhythm. If a patient has been in atrial fibrillation
for longer than a few days, there is a small risk that this may be associated with emboli leaving the left
atrium. This is why amiodarone is reserved for patients with cardiovascular compromise that is clinically
significant.
If amiodarone is commenced, the full dose should be administered even if the rhythm reverts to sinus
rhythm, unless severe hypotension or bradycardia occurs.
Amiodarone is often described as relatively contraindicated in the presence of a prolonged QT interval,
but this only applies to long-term administration.
When diluting amiodarone with 0.9% sodium chloride the solution will go slightly cloudy. This does not
adversely affect the amiodarone.
Avoid shaking the ampoule because this will cause the solution to froth.

Additional information
General principles

Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is the presence of a palpable pulse, or clear signs of
spontaneous circulation (such as non-agonal breathing, normal ETCO2 or active movement) in the
absence of CPR.
The most important aspects of post cardiac arrest care are to maintain an adequate airway, breathing and
circulation, avoiding hypoxia, hyperventilation and hypotension.
In the first few minutes following ROSC, the patient’s physiological state is often quite unstable and it is
important to monitor the patient closely and intervene as required. It is appropriate to prepare for
transport during this time and to complete the post cardiac arrest checklist, but do not immediately
commence transport unless the patient has an unresolved time critical problem.
Targeted temperature management
Targeted temperature management (TTM) and the avoidance of hyperthermia may improve outcomes
following cardiac arrest in patients who remain unconscious.
If core temperature monitoring is available, target a temperature of 35-36°C. Following ROSC, most
patients covered with a single blanket will achieve a temperature of approximately 36°C. If core
temperature monitoring is not available, cover the patient with a blanket.
It is useful to document the patient’s tympanic temperature post ROSC, but this is not a priority.
There is no role for active warming unless the patient has had a cardiac arrest secondary to hypothermia.
There is no role for active cooling unless the patient has hyperthermia.
Blood pressure
There is reduced blood flow to the brain post cardiac arrest, even if blood pressure is normal.
Any fall in blood pressure will further reduce blood flow to the brain and this is why a systolic blood

RSI (Rapid Sequence Intubation)
RSI is indicated for a patient with a GCS less than or equal to 10, and
Clinically significant compromise of airway or ventilation, or
A clinical trajectory requiring RSI.

Use the PODCASTS acronym to consider factors contributing to the balance of risk prior to proceeding
with RSI.

P

Predicted difficulty of intubation.

O

Oxygenation and ventilation (severity of impairment).

D

Distance (time) to hospital.

C

Comorbidities that limit life expectancy.

A

Age, particularly those aged less than 5 years, or greater than 75 years.

S

Shock.

T

Trajectory of clinical course.

S

Special circumstances.

RSI procedure
Ensure adequate preparation and resuscitation before commencing RSI.
Utilise the RSI checklist.
Administer 2 mcg/kg of fentanyl IV (up to a maximum of 200 mcg) immediately prior to ketamine if the
patient has:
Traumatic brain injury, or
Suspected intracranial pathology, or
Hypertension (SBP > 150 mmHg in an adult).
Withhold fentanyl if the above clinical indications are not present, or there are signs of shock.
Administer 2 mg/kg of ketamine IV (up to a maximum of 200 mg) for most patients.
Consider reducing the dose to 1 mg/kg if:
There are signs of shock, or
Sedative medicines have already been administered or taken.

General principles
The primary goal of performing RSI is to improve patient outcomes by securing the airway, treating
hypoxia and controlling ventilation to prevent hypercarbia. This is particularly important in patients who
are unconscious post cardiac arrest or have severe TBI, because secondary brain injury worsens long-term
outcomes.
Personnel calling for backup from a CCP must consider how long it will take for backup to arrive. To be
appropriately utilised, such backup must arrive at least 15 minutes faster than the patient can be
transported to an appropriate hospital.
Including the clinical trajectory of the patient in the decision to perform RSI requires good clinical
judgment. A clinical trajectory requiring RSI requires that the expectation is that the patient is likely to be
admitted to an ICU ventilated, for example because the patient has severe TBI or is post cardiac arrest. A
clinical trajectory that the patient may require intubation and ventilation for a procedure, such as surgery
or a CT scan, is not usually considered an indication for RSI.
Whenever feasible, an ICP or second CCP should be utilised as a dedicated assistant.
If hypoxia is severe or the patient is at high risk of desaturation, consider oxygen via nasal prongs at 15
litres/minute during laryngoscopy.
PODCASTS acronym
The decision to perform RSI requires clinical judgement that considers all factors contributing to the
balance of risk for each patient. Use of the PODCASTS mnemonic provides a structure to help ensure key
factors are considered. Personnel must have a low threshold for seeking clinical advice if unsure.

P

Predicted difficulty of intubation. If the intubation is predicted to be difficult, the balance of risk
usually shifts toward the RSI occurring in hospital.

O

Oxygenation and ventilation (severity of impairment). If there is severe impairment of oxygenation
or ventilation (particularly oxygenation) that cannot be managed with basic airway manoeuvres
and/or adjuncts, the balance of risk usually shifts toward RSI occurring out of hospital.

D

Distance (time) to hospital. If the time to the most appropriate hospital, including extrication time,
is prolonged, the balance of risks usually shifts toward RSI occurring out of hospital. There is no
time ‘cut off’, but it should be unusual to perform RSI within 15 minutes of the most appropriate
hospital.

C

Comorbidities that limit life expectancy. The presence of life limiting comorbidities usually shifts the
balance of risk toward RSI occurring in hospital, because of the implications for ongoing treatment
such as admission to an intensive care unit.

A

Age. For those aged less than 5 years or greater than 75 years, the balance of risk usually shifts

Shock. The presence of shock, particularly hypovolaemic shock, usually shifts the balance of risk

Choice and dosing of medicines
Fentanyl should usually be administered immediately prior to ketamine when performing RSI for patients
with traumatic brain injury, suspected intracranial pathology (for example haemorrhagic stroke) or
hypertension (a SBP greater than 150 mmHg in an adult or a SBP significantly higher than normal in a
child).
This is because fentanyl may reduce the rise in BP and/or intracranial pressure, that may occur with
laryngoscopy and intubation.
2 mcg/kg (to a maximum of 200 mcg) is an appropriate dose for most patients.
However, fentanyl may contribute to hypotension. For this reason, fentanyl should be withheld if
there are signs of shock.
Ketamine is always administered during RSI.
2 mg/kg (to a maximum of 200 mg) is an appropriate dose for most patients.
Although ketamine usually produces a small rise in BP, ketamine may cause a fall in BP if shock is
present. For this reason, reduce the dose to 1 mg/kg if there are signs of shock.
Consider reducing the dose to 1 mg/kg if sedative medicines have been administered, or taken. For
example, consider reducing the dose to 1 mg/kg if:
A sedative dose of ketamine has been administered as part of a delayed sequence intubation, or
The patient has taken sedative medicines.
Do not reduce the dose of ketamine in the setting of RSI for prolonged seizures. Even though
midazolam will have been administered, an anticonvulsant dose of ketamine is required.
Neuromuscular blockade is always administered during RSI.
2 mg/kg of rocuronium or suxamethonium (to a maximum of 200 mg) is an appropriate dose for all
patients.

Delayed sequence intubation

Delayed sequence intubation is a term used to describe the administration of sedation prior to
embarking on the RSI procedure.
Delayed sequence intubation is indicated if the patient meets criteria for RSI, but is agitated and/or
combative to a level that is preventing safe preparation prior to RSI:
Administer sufficient ketamine (usually 1 mg/kg IV) to gain control of the agitation.
Once control is gained, ensure adequate pre-oxygenation and complete the RSI checklist.
Perform RSI and consider reducing the dose of ketamine, considering the dose of medicines already
administered.
Crash RSI
Rarely, a patient may be deteriorating so rapidly that there is a high risk of death occuring prior to
performing RSI, and a truncated (or ‘crash’) approach should be undertaken.
Task one person to provide as much as pre-oxygenation as possible.
Utilise the crash RSI checklist.
Omit fentanyl and administer ketamine and neuromuscular blockade.
Intubation without medicines
For the majority of unconscious patients not in cardiac arrest, the risks of intubation without medicines
outweigh the benefits.
Intubation and ventilation without medicines must only occur if the patient has a GCS of 3 and ineffective
breathing.
Measurement of end tidal CO2 (ETCO2)
Intubation must not be attempted unless measurement of ETCO2 via capnography is immediately
available.
